title: Non-Negotiable Sovereignty, the Basis of Foreign Policy, Foreign Minister Says
author: Andrea Becerril and Georgina Saldierna
content:
_This article by[Andrea
Becerril](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Andrea%20Becerril) and [Georgina
Saldierna](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Georgina%20Saldierna) originally
appeared in the [October 15, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/2026/10/15/politica/007n1pol), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

From the floor of the Senate, Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco Álvarez stated
that at moments of greatest complexity for diplomacy, when we are living
through “times of pressure, noise and uncertainty,” Mexico relies on a foreign
policy of State that starts from the conviction that sovereignty and the
national interest “are not negotiated, are not limited and are not
subordinated to anyone.”

Appearing before the upper chamber for the review of President Claudia
Sheinbaum’s second State of the Nation Report, the head of the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs (SRE) emphasized that if anything sums up the year he reported
on yesterday, “it is that cooperation and sovereignty advance together: we
cooperate more than ever and we always decide as Mexicans.”

> For a country whose history is marked by foreign invasions and
> interventions, international law is our main weapon.
>
> Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco

“Each of the **36 daily visits by our consular staff to a detention center in
the United States** , each agreement that opens a market for our producers,
each principle we uphold in international forums pursue the same goal: to
guarantee that the people of Mexico are always the ones who decide their
destiny.”

He stressed that migrants are the priority, and in the face of “the
regrettable cases of Mexicans injured or killed in custody or during
operations in the United States, we have stepped up efforts to clarify the
facts and demand [accountability] with the greatest rigor and responsibility.

“Each case has a first and last name, each family deserves an answer; this
foreign ministry will seek them all, one by one,” he underlined. In addition
to being in the detention centers every day, he explained, **16 diplomatic
notes were sent to the State Department and 20 complaints to the prosecutors’
offices in charge of the investigations** , and communication is maintained
with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.

He emphasized that with the United States “we hold dialogue and cooperate in
all fields, especially in security, always on the basis of respect for
sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

He stated that monthly fentanyl seizures at the southern border of our
northern neighbor **decreased 67 percent between October 2024 and August
2026**.

In addition, “Mexico has captured **five members of the FBI’s list of the 10
most wanted fugitives** ,” an “unprecedented result in the region, and has
taken more than 35,000 firearms out of circulation, nearly 80 percent of them
from the United States.”

To PAN Senator Marko Cortés, who argued that President Donald Trump halted the
extension of the T-MEC [USMCA] because of Mexico’s refusal to extradite the
governor of Sinaloa on leave, Rubén Rocha Moya, and other former officials of
the state, he responded that “that has nothing to do with it.

“The T-MEC is a trilateral treaty, and I would ask what relationship Canada
has with these extradition issues, which are bilateral in nature.” He added
that negotiations between our country and Washington “continue through formal
tables that are being held,” and are not mixed with political or security
issues.

Earlier, he made clear that “international cooperation in security is an
important tool and has only one point of entry: the one set by law, through
the Foreign Ministry.”

Velasco also refuted the assertion by Cortés —and by other _blanquiazul_ [PAN]
senators— that “Mexico’s international prestige has collapsed.” On the
contrary, he responded, “there is enormous respect for our diplomacy, for
President Sheinbaum” and for the traditional foreign policy.

As an example, he detailed that today the country is expanding its
preferential access to the world’s large markets, with the review of the T-MEC
and with the Modernized Global Agreement with the European Union, already
signed.

Morena senators Alejandro Murat and Juan Carlos Loera de la Rosa demanded that
the PAN member stop lying and disparaging a foreign policy that has delivered
results. “Mexico has a fundamental leadership, as shown by Foreign Minister
Velasco’s presence at the UN in defense of substantive equality,” said the
former.

In his closing remarks, [Velasco] highlighted that beyond ideological
differences, unity is required to protect Mexicans abroad, strengthen economic
relations and consolidate an active and constructive presence in the world.
